Make the harbour journey easier
The passenger problem
Passengers lose time at entrances, transfers and platform exits. The proposed improvement programme focuses on the moments where uncertainty interrupts an otherwise straightforward journey.
The service response
Clarify destinations before boarding and place directions where decisions happen. Use consistent station names across platform signs, printed maps and passenger announcements.
The intended result
A clearer journey should reduce hesitation and missed connections. Establish a baseline first, then compare passenger observations after the pilot changes are installed.
Three priorities for the pilot
ENTRY
Distribute arriving passengers along the platform by making the second entrance easier to find. Place the first directional sign before the approach divides.
TRANSFER
Show the connecting platform at the point where passengers leave the train. Repeat the direction at each turn through the station passage.
EXIT
Identify the useful carriage end before arrival at the quay. Give passengers enough time to move safely toward the ferry connection.
The journey has three decision points
Before boarding
Passengers need the correct destination and stopping pattern. Display short-turn services clearly so colour alone does not imply that every train reaches the docks.
During the transfer
Passengers need the next direction immediately after leaving the train. Put the connecting service name above the sightline of people waiting on the platform.
At the destination
Passengers need a useful street landmark and the correct exit. Add a local inset where walls or closed gates make the walking route indirect.
Compare the improvement options
Signage refresh
A targeted signage update can address the most immediate points of confusion. It requires clear placement decisions and coordination with existing station information.
Entrance changes
A second entrance could distribute crowds more effectively. Evaluate walking routes, accessibility and operational constraints before committing to a permanent physical alteration.
Recommended sequence
Begin with a reversible signage pilot at the interchange. Use the observed passenger response to decide whether a larger entrance project is justified.
Measure the experience on the platform
Transfer time
Record the elapsed time from leaving the train to reaching the connecting platform. Compare similar arrivals so the observation reflects the route.
Wrong turns
Count passengers who reverse direction at the main passage junction. Note whether each event happens before or after they encounter the directional sign.
Passenger confidence
Ask a short question after the transfer about the clarity of the route. Keep the wording consistent across baseline and pilot observation periods.
A compact pilot with clear ownership
Include three stations representing entry, transfer and exit problems. This keeps the pilot manageable while covering distinct stages of the passenger journey.
Observe two operating periods at each location. Include a weekday commute and a weekend market service to capture different movement patterns and luggage needs.
Assign one accountable station lead to each site. The lead records installation issues, coordinates observations and confirms that temporary signs remain in place.
Coordinate the teams that deliver it
Station operations
Review the proposed sign locations against passenger flows and routine maintenance access. Confirm that installation can happen without obstructing safe movement through the station.
Passenger information
Approve consistent naming and destinations across every pilot sign. Check the printed message against announcements and digital departure information before the first installation.
Accessibility review
Walk the proposed route with accessibility reviewers. Confirm readable placement and an appropriate step-free alternative wherever the shortest route depends on stairs.
Keep the pilot safe and reversible
Conflicting information
New directions could disagree with existing signs. Audit each decision point before installation and remove temporary messages that create an ambiguous choice.
Service disruption
Engineering work could change the route during observation. Record operating conditions and repeat the session when disruption prevents a meaningful comparison with baseline.
Maintenance ownership
A damaged temporary sign can undermine the whole route. Assign an inspection owner and keep replacement artwork available throughout the pilot period.
Six weeks from baseline to decision
WEEKS 1–2
Observe the current passenger journey and agree the priority decision points. Complete the sign audit, accessibility walk and baseline measurement before installation begins.
WEEKS 3–4
Install temporary signs and observe the same journeys again. Record passenger questions, operational issues and any adjustments made during the first days.
WEEKS 5–6
Compare the findings with the baseline and review them with station teams. Recommend which changes to retain, revise or investigate through a larger project.
Authorize the pilot and review the evidence
Decision requested
Approve a three-station pilot with temporary signage and structured observation. Confirm the accountable leads before the installation schedule is released to station teams.
Evidence required
Bring baseline and pilot observations to the review together. Include transfer times, wrong turns, passenger feedback and any material changes in operating conditions.
Next decision
Use the findings to choose permanent improvements and scope any further investigation. Document the reasons for each recommendation so the rollout remains accountable.
